newsitem.title: ZAIRE: War-torn Zaire debates changing prime minister.
newsitem.headline: War-torn Zaire debates changing prime minister.

text.p: Zaire's politicians debated the composition of a crisis government on Friday, with President Mobutu Sese Seko's supporters divided on whether to keep Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo.
Inhabitants of Zaire's sprawling capital awaited news as political parties met and swapped ideas on the government, due to be announced within the next day.
State radio said the mobile telephone network, Zaire's only working communications system, was overloaded as politicians tried to manoeuvre into the government.
Banza Mukalayi, vice-president of Mobutu's Popular Revolutionary Movement (MPR), reported a heated debate within the party on whether to retain Kengo at the head of the new government.
Protesters had demanded the removal of Kengo, who is part Tutsi, early in the Tutsi-led rebellion in eastern Zaire that has shaken the country over the past two months.
"One current of opinion appears to be leaning in favour of the incumbent prime minister. They say he represents a certain stability," Banza told Reuters.

"Another group is saying, that the expectations of the people are clear," he added, indicating that some MPR members now favoured reinstating Mobutu's and Kengo's long-term political rival, Etienne Tshisekedi.

Mobutu, who has dominated the nation since seizing power in 1965, returned home from Europe on Tuesday saying he was cutting short his convalescence after cancer surgery because of the Tutsi-led revolt in the east.
His supporters have a majority in the central African nation's transitional parliament.
"So far we are not involved. We are waiting for the big man to meet our big man and then we will know which way things are going," Gilbert Mundele, a Tshisekedi spokesman told Reuters.
Mundele said Mobutu would probably meet Tshisekedi on Sunday -- after the 48 hour deadline Mobutu set for a new government at a meeting of party leaders on Thursday.

Tshisekedi, replaced by a Mobutu appointee in 1993, has bitterly contested Kengo's right to the job of prime minister. He and Mobutu held a "reconciliation" meeting before Mobutu's return from France this week.
Witnesses said demonstrators carrying posters of Tshisekedi and calling for his reappointment as prime minister demonstrated in central Kinshasa on Friday afternoon.
"They were about 200 of them shouting 'Tshisekedi or nothing.' The military arrived in jeeps and as soon as they climbed down the demonstrators ran away," Reuters cameraman Clotaire Achi said.
Tshisekedi turned up at the meeting with Mobutu on Thursday but refused to participate because the leader of a breakaway faction of his party, Frederic Kibassa Maliba, was present.
Since his return, Mobutu has shuffled the military high command, bringing in a popular general, Mahele Bokoungo, respected by both regular troops and the wider population.
Mahele is one of the rare top generals in Zaire who has earned his senior rank on the battlefield and not through family ties to the president.
But Zaire watchers say if Mobutu wants to resume full control of the sprawling, anarchic nation he also has to broker a political solution.
